tagline.text: Manila's largest public cemetery, where presidents and heroes rest and thousands live

location.label: Location
location.text: Santa Cruz, Manila; entrance at the corner of Blumentritt Street and Dimasalang Street (another main gate on A. Bonifacio Avenue)

best_season.label: Best time to visit

budget.label: Budget

children.text: Manila North Cemetery is a municipal cemetery laid out in 1904, a vast burial ground of about 54 hectares on the northern edge of the city. With the tombs of three presidents and other historic figures, Egyptian-inspired and Art Deco mausoleums, and a community of thousands who live among the graves, it is a place where you can walk through Manila's modern history.
Manila North Cemetery is a public cemetery owned and run by the Manila city government, on the northern edge of the Santa Cruz district. According to Wikipedia it covers about
54 ha

(about 130 acres), making it one of the largest cemeteries in Metro Manila. La Loma Cemetery and the Manila Chinese Cemetery sit right next to it, so together the three form an entire city district given over to the dead.

The cemetery was laid out in 1904 as the "Cementerio del Norte" (Spanish for North Cemetery). It is said to have been part of La Loma Cemetery originally and was separated as an exclusively Catholic burial ground. The whole area was once known as Paang Bundok, the spot José Rizal chose as his own final resting place. Today a barangay called Paang Bundok lies across from the cemetery.

The appeal of the North Cemetery for travelers is twofold. The first is history. Three presidents, Sergio Osmeña, Manuel Roxas, and Ramon Magsaysay, are buried here, along with writers, painters, mayors, and film stars from modern Philippine history, and there are memorial mausoleums for veterans of the revolution and for victims of World War II. The second is architecture. You can see every style in one cemetery, from plain painted tombs to large mausoleums decorated with carved reliefs and colored glass, and standout works such as a family mausoleum guarded by sphinxes at its entrance and an Art Deco-flavored pylon tomb.

It is also important to know that this is a living neighborhood. According to a 2025 AFP report (carried by Gulf News and others) and Wikipedia, about 6,000 informal settlers live inside the cemetery, many of them working as caretakers of mausoleums. They sometimes point visitors in the right direction or act as informal guides, sharing the oral history of the place. If you treat it not as a curiosity but as someone's home, and move through it with respect, it becomes one of the most meaningful experiences in Manila. Most visitors come around All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day (known locally as Undas, around November 1–2 each year). Hundreds of thousands of people turn out, the cemetery takes on a festival atmosphere, and vendors selling flowers and candles line the roads. On ordinary days it is quiet and well suited to walking, photography, and history tours. This guide covers both situations.

The tomb of Sergio Osmeña (1878–1961), the fourth president of the Philippines, is described as lying along the main avenue. Ramon Magsaysay (1907–1957) opened the gates of Malacañang Palace to the public and became known as the "president of the masses," and Manuel Roxas is also buried here. Signage changes from year to year, so the fastest way to find a tomb is to ask at the information desk near the entrance or a local guide.

blocks.title: Mausoleum of the Veterans of the Revolution

children.text: The Mausoleum of the Veterans of the Revolution is a national monument honoring veterans of the Philippine Revolution and the Philippine–American War. The 1984 film Bulaklak sa City Jail is said to have been shot inside this mausoleum. It is a good place to reflect briefly on how the last generation of the independence struggle is remembered.

Completed in 1915, this mausoleum was designed by the brothers Arcadio and Juan Arellano and is known for its Egyptian-inspired design and two sphinxes at the entrance. The sight of Egyptian temple style in a Philippine cemetery is unusual, which makes it a popular photo spot. Before getting close, ask a caretaker or nearby resident whether photography is fine.

This pylon-shaped tomb with Art Deco elements was designed by National Artist Juan Nakpil. His father, Julio Nakpil, composed the Katipunan anthem, and Julio's wife, Gregoria de Jesus, was the widow of Andrés Bonifacio and is known as the "Muse of the Katipunan." The Nakpil family tombs are a place where Philippine independence history and modern architectural history meet.

blocks.title: World War II victims' memorial mausoleum

children.text: A memorial mausoleum honors 29 Manila residents executed by the Japanese Army in 1944, whose remains are said to have been interred here on March 9, 1947. Wikipedia also records accounts that more than 2,000 unarmed civilians were killed here between October and November 1944, but the period (October–November or December) and the toll (over 2,000, or 27 in a separate entry) differ between listings and could not be confirmed from independent sources, so treat it as an unverified account. Figures may differ between sources, so read the information boards as well.

blocks.title: Tombs of writers, artists, and mayors

children.text: Buried here are the poet Amado Hernández, the painter Félix Resurrección Hidalgo, the statesman Claro M. Recto, Arcadio Arellano, and former Manila mayors Arsenio Lacson and Alfredo Lim. The tombs of film giants Fernando Poe Sr. and Jr. and Susan Roces are also here. That is why this one cemetery reads like a biographical dictionary.
This four-story building opened on October 24, 2016, after construction began in February of that year at a cost of about
. It has a floor area of about
, with 4,088 niches and 1,218 slots for coffins. It is a modern facility that shows how cremation and niche burial are taking hold in a big city where burial land is running out.

This is an extension of the cemetery developed as a joint venture between the City of Manila and a private consortium. It offers a tidy, park-style cemetery in contrast to the traditional large mausoleums. Check locally for its exact location and conditions of use.

items.title: Weekday half-day cemetery walk
items.subtitle: Presidential tombs and mausoleum architecture on foot

children.text: Leave from LRT-1 Blumentritt Station around
and walk to the entrance, a distance reported at
about 15 minutes
on foot. It is best to arrive before the sun gets hot.

Let the administration office near the entrance know you are visiting, and check the information boards and the map. If you ask a resident for informal guidance, decide in advance how much you will give as thanks.
Follow the central avenue to look for the tombs of presidents Osmeña, Magsaysay, Roxas, and others. Markers may or may not be present at each tomb, so it helps to bring a list of names.
Visit the Tuason-Legarda family mausoleum (the sphinxes), the Bautista-Nakpil pylon, and the Mausoleum of the Veterans of the Revolution in turn, comparing their architectural styles.
There is little shade, so sort out your water and snacks near the entrance and leave the cemetery. Have lunch on nearby streets or around La Loma.

Exact weekday opening hours differ by source. The cemetery is generally said to be open from early morning to late afternoon, but check the latest notices from the Manila North Cemetery administration office before you go.

items.title: Three-cemetery full-day route
items.subtitle: From the North Cemetery to the Chinese Cemetery and La Loma

children.text: Start at the North Cemetery entrance and walk slowly through the presidential tombs and main mausoleums.
Cross to the neighboring Manila Chinese Cemetery to see its temples and traditional-style mausoleums. It is covered in detail in its own entry.
For lunch, head out to restaurants near a nearby jeepney stop or toward Binondo.
Walk around the La Loma Church area and take a short look at the atmosphere of La Loma Cemetery. Check locally whether it is open.
Head back to an LRT-1 station before the light fades. Avoid walking alone around the cemeteries at dusk.
During All Saints' Day, private vehicle access is restricted and the crowds are very large, so this route is practically impossible. In that period, aim only for the North Cemetery.

From central Manila (Ermita, Malate, Intramuros), take a northbound LRT-1 train and get off at Blumentritt Station or Abad Santos Station. According to 2026 guidance, the cemetery entrance is at the corner of Blumentritt Street and Dimasalang Street, a short walk from the station.
From Blumentritt Station to the entrance is reported at about
15 minutes
on foot. In hot weather you can also take a tricycle or jeepney.
The first LRT-1 train is reported to run at
on weekends and holidays. Check weekday operating hours and fares locally.
From Makati, the usual route is to take the MRT-3 or a bus to a nearby transfer station and change to LRT-1. Check the transfer details on a map app at the time.
From Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), a taxi or Grab straight to the cemetery is the simplest option. Travel time varies greatly with traffic, so allow plenty of time.
You can also go first to your hotel in Manila and then take LRT-1.
In Manila, jeepneys and buses run along Rizal Avenue and A. Bonifacio Avenue, and taxis and Grab are also available.
During All Saints' Day, some roads around Blumentritt, Dimasalang, and Maceda are closed, so use public transport and do not bring a car.
Road closures differ from year to year. Check the latest traffic notices from the city of Manila and the police.
For ordinary visits, the dry season from December to May is best for walking. There is little shade, so midday in March to May is very hot. An early-morning visit is safer and better for photos.

During All Saints' Day and All Souls' Day from late October to early November, Manila's municipal cemeteries are at their busiest of the year. In 2025, reports said about 30,000 people visited the North Cemetery on a single Sunday, and officials expect far larger crowds over the whole period. It is a meaningful time for those who want to experience local culture, but be especially prepared for crowds and pickpockets.

There is almost no accommodation suited to travelers right next to the North Cemetery. Most visitors stay in Ermita and Malate, Intramuros, or Makati and make a day trip by LRT-1 or Grab. Hotel prices and reviews change with the season, so check recent reviews on a booking site.

There is not much food inside or just outside the cemetery. On ordinary days the stalls near the entrance are said to be limited, so bring water and snacks, and eat in Binondo's Chinatown or at restaurants elsewhere in the city. During All Saints' Day, residents sell drinks and snacks and rent out toilets, but facilities are basic, so do not expect much.
Dress modestly, in clothes that cover your shoulders and knees, and wear comfortable sneakers. Many paths are uneven and narrow.
Ask permission before photographing a mausoleum or a person. Photography for personal use is generally allowed, but do not photograph people praying at family tombs or residents' homes.
There is little shade and few benches, so bring a hat, sunscreen, and water. Basic restrooms are reported near the entrance.
If you visit during All Saints' Day, go early in the morning, leave large bags and valuables behind, and carry small bills.
If someone offers informal guidance, tip them and agree on a time in advance so you are not held for long. You can also walk alone, keeping to the main roads.

If you want to dig deeper into the history, check whether a heritage group or a walking-tour operator (for example, Carlos Celdran's "Walk This Way" in the past) has a tour scheduled. In the past, tours combining the North Cemetery, the Chinese Cemetery, and La Loma Cemetery have been held.
Around All Saints' Day, the city of Manila sometimes opens an online grave finder, so if you are looking for a family grave, check the announcements.
This is a place where families rest and where thousands of people make their homes. Do not make loud noise, drink alcohol, or photograph people without permission.
During All Saints' Day (October 29 to November 2 in 2026), opening hours were extended to
and vehicles were banned. This changes every year, so check the notices.
During Undas, firearms, sharp objects such as knives, alcohol, pets, loudspeakers and sound equipment, and gambling are prohibited. Do not bring them.
On crowded days pickpockets increase and it is easy to get lost. Keep your phone and wallet in front of you.
Avoid walking alone after dusk or entering quiet inner sections.
Some areas are rundown and lack signage. Check the current opening hours and rules with the local administration office and the latest notices from the city of Manila.
The adjoining
Manila Chinese Cemetery
is known for its temples and ornate mausoleums and can be reached on foot.
If you want to combine a meal and shopping,
Binondo
is close by. Travel time depends on traffic; go by LRT or taxi.
You can continue your Manila history tour at
Intramuros
, the walled city from the Spanish colonial era.
If you want to see more cemetery architecture and war memory in Manila, you can visit the
Manila American Cemetery
in the same week. It is far away and needs a separate itinerary.
